title: Four Arrested After 18 Elephants Die in Kenya's Amboseli Ecosystem
excerpt: Kenyan authorities seized chemicals and detained four suspects as investigations into suspected cyanide poisoning of elephants near Amboseli National Park deepened.
body:
• Police arrested four suspects and seized chemicals in the investigation into 18 elephant deaths in Kenya's Amboseli ecosystem since June 24
  • Preliminary lab results point to cyanide poisoning from pesticide-contaminated tomatoes on farms bordering Amboseli National Park
  • Victims were predominantly adult female elephants and calves that showed partial paralysis before dying within one to two days
  • Wildlife experts have questioned the pesticide theory, noting no deaths among other animals in the area

Arrests and Seizures

Kenyan police have arrested four suspects in connection with the deaths of 18 elephants in the Amboseli ecosystem, Kenya's tourism and wildlife ministry announced. Authorities also seized assorted substances, including chemicals believed to have come from a neighboring country, during a search in Tikondo, Loitoktok sub-county, about 220 kilometers southeast of Nairobi.

https://x.com/citizentvkenya/status/2091234745057161374

A Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) spokesperson confirmed the four have since been released on bail. Investigators are pursuing a fifth individual believed to have information relevant to the case.

The ministry cautioned that the arrests and recovered substances "did not in themselves establish criminal culpability" and that investigations remain ongoing.

A Growing Death Toll

The first 15 elephant deaths were recorded between June 24 and July 24 in Amboseli National Park, Kimana Sanctuary, and the Kuku Ranch area. Three more deaths followed, bringing the toll to 18. Ten of the elephants showed symptoms of partial paralysis, leaving them unable to stand before dying within one to two days. Five carcasses were too decomposed or scavenged for cause-of-death analysis.

The condition primarily affected adult females and calves, with only one adult male among the dead — a pattern that puzzled investigators, since male elephants are more likely to raid crops.

"We need to know what is killing our elephants."

— Maasai community elder Papatiti

Competing Theories

Preliminary laboratory results from the University of Nairobi detected a potential toxic substance, with earlier indications suggesting cyanide poisoning from pesticide-contaminated tomatoes grown on farms bordering the national park. A 2024 report by the Route to Food Initiative had documented cyanide-based insecticide use at farms in Kimana town, a major tomato-producing area.

However, several wildlife experts have challenged the pesticide theory. Paula Kahumbu, conservationist and head of Wildlife Direct, highlighted the "lack of evidence" supporting it, noting that few adult male elephants — the most likely crop raiders — had died. Separate tests by the Government Chemist were negative for the toxins initially examined, with further testing underway.

KWS has requested the Pest Control Products Board to lead a multi-agency technical team to investigate whether crop-protection chemicals were improperly used, stored, or disposed of in the wider Amboseli ecosystem.

Human-Wildlife Conflict

The Amboseli ecosystem spans the national park and surrounding community land in southern Kenya near the Tanzanian border, providing critical habitat and movement corridors for elephants and other wildlife beneath Mount Kilimanjaro. The area has a long history of human-wildlife conflict, with elephants frequently wandering onto farmland in search of food and water.

The tragedy highlights the mounting tension between expanding agricultural land and conservation in one of East Africa's most iconic wildlife regions. Kenya's elephant population — estimated at around 36,000 — has been slowly recovering from decades of poaching, making the mass die-off particularly alarming for conservationists.

"The reported cyanide poisoning must be urgently and thoroughly investigated, and those responsible must be held fully accountable under the law."

— Ben Wandago, International Fund for Animal Welfare East Africa Director

What's Next

Environmental investigations continue, including analysis of water sources and other potential contaminants within the affected area. KWS has assured the public that there is no evidence the condition poses any risk to human health or can be transmitted to people. Community leaders fear the death toll may be underestimated and that the affliction could also be affecting elephants across the border in Tanzania.
